rv.q: Baker renews the theme for the early 20th century with perspicacity and humor.
'Partnership' charms regardless, offering a gentle reminder about not letting work overtake your life.
Mint’s latest, Partnership by Elizabeth Baker, is quite a revelation, both in the quality of the writing and the eye-opening perceptions it reveals about working women more than a century ago.
It's good to have Elizabeth Baker back in the mix.
The Mint’s production is a faithful, beautifully constructed staging of a play that may not truly be worth such effort.
As a romantic comedy, this 'Partnership' is regrettably a one-sided affair.
Women theatergoers may appreciate a period play which puts the female roles front and center, but this play is too bland and inoffensive to make much impact.
Directed by Jackson Grace Gay, this Partnership simply doesn’t meet the Mint’s usual high standards.
As is the case with most Mint shows, this is a very competent production of a play that has earned its obscurity.
I urge you to stay past the slower expository first interval though as acts two and three give this play value for today...

...‘Partnership’ more modestly fulfills the Mint’s mission of producing ‘worthwhile plays from the past that have been lost or forgotten’...There are some awkwardly written sequences, but all-around good acting and adept direction by Gay make the journey through Baker’s England a pleasant and rewarding one.
And, speaking of stretching, I hope that the Mint’s infatuation with Miss Baker has reached its limit.
The Mint completes its wonderful “Meet Miss Baker” trilogy with Partnership, another exquisite production of a work by early-twentieth-century playwright and office typist Elizabeth Baker.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Mint Theater revival of Baker's 1917 play about a businesswoman weighing a practical marriage proposal. While many praise the company's mission and the play's timely themes about work-life balance, others find it dated.
